item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
item.description:
Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado

Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.

Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. The tornado caused extensive damage, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states have requested federal funding assistance after the extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.

item.description:
UKMTO says 11 ships attacked in week to 4 Nov in Hormuz, Arabian Gulf

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has reported 11 attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Gulf in the seven days to November 4, including incidents that left three vessels sunk.

Eight attacks occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and three in the Arabian Gulf, according to UKMTO's weekly overview. Of the 11 incidents, three vessels continued their voyages, five required assistance and three sank.

The report said one dhow was struck by an unidentified projectile on 2 November, killing one crew member, while 13 others were rescued by local authorities.

A Panama-flagged supply vessel was also struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on 1 November and reportedly sank after a nearby merchant vessel rescued its crew.

A Marshall Islands-flagged tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles in the Arabian Gulf on 4 November, leaving it drifting and requiring assistance from local authorities.

Combined Strait of Hormuz traffic reached 325 transits in the seven-day reporting period, comprising 170 outbound and 155 inbound movements, compared with 277 in the previous week. UKMTO said traffic remained approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels.

Automatic Identification System-observed transits increased to 71 from 64 the previous week, while US-reported facilitated transits remained broadly stable. Around 80 percent of Strait of Hormuz transits continued to involve energy carriers.

UKMTO also reported an increase in vessels using the southern route, although most ships broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route.

In the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb, no attacks on shipping were reported during the week. The last reported attack was on August 24, 65 days earlier. However, Bab el-Mandeb transits remained 24 percent below levels recorded before the Houthi blockade announcement on July 22.

The complaint, submitted to the Dutch National Public Prosecutor's Office on 4 November, names Noam Himmelman, a former member of the Israeli army's Netzah Yehuda Battalion, who is currently in Amsterdam.

HRF alleges that Himmelman was involved in war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide during Israel's war on Gaza. The complaint was filed under the Dutch International Crimes Act, which allows prosecution of international crimes when suspects are present on Dutch territory.

According to HRF, Israeli forces, including the battalion, surrounded schools in Beit Hanoun on 16 April 2024, where thousands of displaced Palestinians had sought shelter. Soldiers allegedly fired on the school complex and detained dozens of men, including elderly people and teenagers, forcing them to strip before taking them away.

HRF says Himmelman documented the arrests in an Instagram story that it subsequently verified and geolocated to a military outpost near the school.

The foundation also alleges that between January and July 2025, the battalion conducted controlled demolitions of residential buildings across Beit Hanoun, contributing to the extensive destruction of the town. Himmelman served with the unit during these operations.

The complaint cites the battalion's previous record of alleged abuses, including the 2022 death of 78-year-old Palestinian-American Omar Assad after he was detained by its soldiers.

Morning update

Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,

If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:

*Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, has said that efforts at mediation between Iran and the United States remain active to prevent escalation, warning that the crisis "cannot be left unresolved".

*Qatar has denied reports that its prime minister said the United States and Iran had failed to reach an agreement to end the war, calling the claims “false and misleading”.

*US President Donald Trump says Washington had made considerable progress in its dealings with Iran, while acknowledging that US forces had carried out limited strikes against targets on the country.

*Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February, says Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia.

*Saudi-led coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the Houthis targeting the Riyadh region, according to spokesperson for the forces, Major General Turki al-Malki. 

*Iran’s army has said air defence force intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over Qeshm Island.

*The United States has urged Americans currently in the Middle East to exercise "heightened vigilance" due to the "increased threat of armed attacks by Houthis and Iranian efforts to target US government officials in the region".

*Israeli forces have carried out raids in several parts of the occupied West Bank and detained at least one person on Saturday, Wafa reported.

*Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty says that he has discussed efforts to "prevent escalation" in the region during his calls with Saudi, UAE and Kuwaiti counterparts. 

*Iranian Army Spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia has said Iran's army will not allow US military bases in the region to be rebuilt.

*The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has said Israeli settlers have carried out a total of 377 attacks on olive harvest across the occupied West Bank since September, a record since 2006 when the UN began recording them.

*The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has reported 11 attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Gulf in the seven days to November 4, including incidents that left three vessels sunk.

*Washington is offering a $20 million reward "and possible relocation" for information about Iran's nuclear programme, the US military said Friday.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Covering Palestine: Historic news clippings reveal US media complicity in Israel's crimes
item.description:
Covering Palestine: Historic news clippings reveal US media complicity in Israel's crimes

Submitted by Fleur Hargreaves on Wed, 10/28/2026 - 13:45
An archive of American newspaper excerpts documents how Israel’s occupation was reported before 7 October 2023
A clipping from the San Francisco Examiner with the headline “Arab activist killed by Santa Ana bomb” from 12 October 1985
Off

For years, mainstream media has been criticised for its failure to report accurately on Israel’s genocide in Gaza, allowing Israel to commit crimes with impunity. 

In July the UN special rapporteur for the Palestinian territories, Fransesca Albanese, released a report about the media complicity in genocide.

Her report details how the systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists, Israeli media’s incitement, and the legitimisation from international coverage have facilitated genocide and obstructed accountability. 

Outlets relied heavily on Israeli sources, using the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 to justify Israel’s subsequent onslaught and present the conflict as though it began exclusively with the attack.

It was frustration with this narrative that prompted Maria Robles, an independent researcher and artist, to begin research into archival American newspaper stories.

She wanted to “share the reality” of what was happening in Palestine through “public history and public memory - not based on opinion, but aggregating existing materials, existing research, existing journalism and making it as accessible as possible to the public”.

Over three years, Robles collated more than 3,000 clippings from almost 700 papers dating from 1724 to 2023, using online archives and physical records, and in doing so, establishing Covering Palestine.

Robles had previously worked on a research campaign to raise awareness about the history of slavery in New York using publicly available archive material.

“Covering Palestine similarly is about education or access to it, being a tool. So is data,” she told Middle East Eye. “I think both of them move us toward liberation, one step at a time.” 

The website allows users to filter material by year, newspaper and subject, tracing patterns, names and key events.

She hopes the archive will help the public understand Palestine’s history prior to 2023 and allow researchers and organisations to “look and understand, criticise and question how the information was shared, and talked about and reported on”.   

From 'colonisation' to 'settlement'

“The media bias has always been there,” Robles explained, but the language used has changed with the times: for example, it was striking that Israel was discussed explicitly as a colonial project when the term was less of a dirty word.

“Plan of colonising Palestine with Jews,” one New York Times headline announced on 6 January 1902.

“Jews set up six colonies,” another said on 24 May 1939. 

In pictures: Life in Palestine from 1890 to 1937
Read More »

In 1926, the Buffalo Jewish Review reported that “Jewish Colonisation will Extend Beyond Palestine Frontier”.

Covering Palestine traces how the word “colonisation” became controversial and was replaced with “settlement”; a shift beginning in the 1920s, with the term having mostly disappeared by 1948.

Today, critics accuse papers such as the New York Times (NYT) of routinely whitewashing Israeli imperialism, comparing headlines describing Israel’s illegal occupation of southern Lebanon as “cementing its foothold” or “plans to control” with much less euphemistic ones about the Russian invasion of Ukraine. 

In an NYT opinion piece, columnist Bret Stephens dismissed the description of Israel as a settler-colonial state as “invidious, hypocritical and historically illiterate” and called Zionism “the oldest continuous anticolonial movement in history”, contradicting how the paper he wrote in once presented it. 

The passive voice 

A 2024 study from The Intercept found a clear pro-Israel bias in mainstream media coverage, particularly the NYT, with outlets consistently applying a double standard when using emotive words such as “massacre” and “slaughter” to describe civilian deaths. 

During the first 100 days of the conflict following 7 October, the NYT used the word “massacre” 124 times to describe violence against Israelis and never against Palestinians; during the first year, CNN used it 225 times for Israelis and 16 times for Palestinians - despite a far higher Palestinian death toll. 

Palestinian deaths, meanwhile, are frequently reported on using the passive voice: a headline from the Washington Post read “Israel’s war in Gaza claims thousands of young lives”. Another stated “more than 1,000 people have been killed in Gaza during ceasefire, Palestinian authorities say”.

This pattern is not new.

On 29 October 1956, Israeli border police shot dead 48 unarmed Palestinian civilians, including 23 children, in Kafr Qasim, who were returning home from their fields for violating a curfew imposed by the Israeli army on the town earlier that day that they had not been informed of. 

Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language

The story was suppressed by Israeli military censorship for 44 days. 

Nothing on Kafr Qasim appears in the archive until 12 December 1956, the day David Ben-Gurion, the prime minister, broke his own ban and told the Knesset.

Of the papers in the archive that carried the disclosure, not one put “massacre” in a headline, and it was not until 13 October 1958, after a military court had convicted eight border police, that the word appeared in a headline to describe the event.

When reports eventually emerged, Covering Palestine’s archive revealed all too familiar patterns of passive and euphemistic language. 

“Israel Discloses Killing of Arabs In Curfew Tift” was how Oregon’s News Review reported on the incident on 12 December 1956. 

Meanwhile, the New York Newsday labelled it “Bare Slaying by Error of 48 Israeli Arabs”: indicating the event was accidental before any investigation had been opened. 

One New York Times headline said “48 Arabs Killed; Israel Penitent”. 

Alongside a scan of the clipping, Robles transcribed the headline, adding citations for researchers and linking to further context. 

She noted the NYT headline was the only one that led with the death toll, but used the passive “killed”, without naming the perpetrator, before turning to “the condition of Israel’s conscience”. 

Censorship

In April 2024, a leaked NYT memo instructed journalists to avoid terms including “genocide”, “ethnic cleansing” and “occupied territory” in their reporting on the conflict. 

Robles noted that historical reports were often explicit about Israeli censorship: a 1980 NYT article declared “Israeli Censorship Strikes a Discordant, Insistent Note”, beginning “this dispatch has been subjected to Israeli censorship”.

By contrast, she said, “now…the reporting has to rationalise, maybe not successfully…why they are reporting it the way they are”, repeating Israeli talking points without acknowledging them, such as “Israel’s right to defend itself” or claims Hamas uses civilians as “human shields”. 

The censorship of the Palestinian press was also reported on by the New York Times, detailing how “Israel Tightens Control Over Arab Newspapers” when Israeli authorities intercepted trucks and confiscated papers being transported for distribution in the West Bank in 1982.

Today, Palestinians document the genocide committed against them directly through social media, reaching international audiences without their language being filtered through American media or Israeli censorship. 

However, Israel’s systematic targeting of Palestinian journalists has made Gaza the deadliest place to be a journalist.

The early reports of Palestinian newspapers being shut down are reflected in Israel’s attacks on journalists today, Robles explained, “not allowing [Palestinians] the opportunity to do their own reporting or speak about what is happening”.

Israel frequently labels Palestinian journalists “terrorists” to justify these attacks - lies that their western colleagues uncritically echo without adequate scrutiny.

Dehumanisation 

Similarly, strikes on Gaza are often reported as “targeting Hamas”, regardless of civilian casualties, while death tolls are attributed to Gaza’s “Hamas-run health ministry”, casting doubt on their reliability.

Yet long before Hamas existed, American papers used dehumanising language to rationalise Israel’s atrocities, diminishing their readers’ empathy for Palestinian victims. 

In July 1972, Palestinian novelist Ghassan Kanafani was killed alongside his teenage niece by a bomb planted in his car in Beirut. 

Reporting on his death, US news outlets presented him as an “Arab Militant leader”, “Revolutionary”, or “Palestinian Guerrilla”, with only one headline in 11 calling him an artist, according to Robles. 

Ghassan Kanafani: The life of a Palestinian writer
Read More »

A central motivation behind Covering Palestine was to humanise Palestinians by documenting their experiences across generations, including rare occasions when they were named or their lives and culture covered without the association with death and suffering. 

“That humanising of people…reminding [the public] that these are really people that these experiences are really happening to” is important to counteract the dehumanisation they face, Robles said.

She also wanted to challenge Zionist myths that Palestine was a “land without people” or not a real country. 

The historical record reveals a people and community that existed for many years prior to Israel’s establishment: one clipping from 1891 described “the Fellaheen [peasants] of Palestine” as “an ancient and historic people”; similarly in 1910 they were referred to as “the aboriginal inhabitants of the Holy Land”.

As genocide seeks to eradicate a people and their past, Robles wants to use Covering Palestine to preserve and expose the history of a place whose story began long before 7 October.
